evidences.title: Emperor and Galilean - review | Theatre | The Guardian
evidences.content:
Ibsen's enormous double-drama has had to bide its time: written between 1868 and 1873, it is only now receiving its British stage premiere, in Jonathan Kent's stunning staging of Ben Power's skilfully edited three-and-a-half-hour version. Whatever doubts I have about the play itself, I would urge anyone interested in Ibsen or the development of drama to see it. After all, it's not likely to come round again in a hurry.

Ibsen uses history to explore ideas, in particular the conflict between determinism and free will. And in this two-part work, spanning the years from AD351 to 363, his focus is on Julian, whom we first see as a nervy 19-year-old living as a virtual prisoner in the Constantinople court of his uncle, the emperor Constantius.

Doubting the state-sanctioned Christianity, Julian escapes to Athens, where he also rejects the pagan philosophers. Revelation comes when he meets the mystic Maxiumus of Ephesus, who sees in Julian a prophet who can transcend the conflict between an earthly empire and a spiritual kingdom. By part two, when Julian has become Roman emperor, we see how this works in practice: in persecution of Christians, prosecution of a war in Persia and in Julian's deluded belief that he is a kind of two-in-one mix of the human and the divine.

But what is Ibsen saying? Writing at a time of intellectual ferment, when the ideas of Marx, Darwin and Nietzsche were changing the world, Ibsen seems to be struggling to articulate a new vision of human freedom: what Shaw, in his essay The Quintessence of Ibsenism, called "the empire of Man asserting the eternal validity of his own will".

While Ibsen could only be alert to the potential dangers of such a philosophy, we know rather too much about the impact the triumphant will would have on 20th century history.

The action of Ibsen's play, in fact, runs counter to its core idea. Ibsen is clearly searching for a new way of living, unshackled by what Julian calls "the doctrines of guilt and misery and denial". Yet what Ibsen actually creates is a powerful defence of Christian idealism. When we see Julian's old friend Gregory blinded and tortured for creating a small church in Antioch, and stoically defying the power-crazed emperor, it is impossible not to be moved.

I was reminded of a story of a young Norwegian sculptor who stunned Ibsen by saying that this was his favourite of all his works because it provided "such a superb account of the triumph of Christianity over heathendom". That seems to me a sign of how, intellectually, the play rebounds on its creator.

It is, however, breathtakingly staged. Paul Brown's design makes brilliant use of the Olivier's drum-revolve to whisk us from Ephesian cellars to Gallic plains and Persian deserts.

Modern costumes and film of aerial bombardment underscore the topicality of a play that deals both with Middle Eastern conflict and the struggle to achieve a world beyond faith. Andrew Scott also gives an heroic performance as Julian. He is especially good at conveying the flailing self-doubt of the young man and evoking the later tyranny without lapsing into the carpet-biting cliche of Hollywood epics.

Ian McDiarmid, meanwhile, invests the mystical Maximus with a faintly Mephistophelian authority, and James McArdle subtly implies a homoerotic relationship between Agathon, Julian's ultimate assassin, and the emperor.

Even though Ibsen's Faustian world-historical play may be several degrees short of a masterpiece, it is still an experience I wouldn't have missed.
